https://www.dw.com/en/us-to-unveil-new-i.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JJFV Iran’s rial currency hit a record low Monday ahead of new sanctions FILE: May 4, 2026] Image: Fatemeh Bahrami/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO Advertisement The US is preparing to unveil a raft of new economic measures targeting Iran and its trade partners amid the stalled six-month old war in the Middle East . Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to announce the measures in a press conference at 1800 GMT on Monday. Iran, a country that has already been living under international sanctions for decades, has vowed to retaliate. In a post on X, Bessent described the sanctions as "the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary." He said US President Donald Trump had "dismantled Iran's military capabilities," destroyed nearly 100% of its military factories and "buried its nuclear program." "We are now entering the endgame," he added. ‘Economic D-Day' Last week, Trump announced what he called an "economic D-Day" for Tehran, threatening harsher sanctions targeting not only Iran but also countries that continue to do business with it. "Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," Bessent said. Already last week, the United Arab Emirates, one of Iran's largest trading partners and its biggest source of imports, announced that it was suspending all trade with Iran. It was not clear if the US measures will include action against China, Russia and India. Ahead of Monday's press conference, China's Foreign Ministry said Beijing was monitoring developments closely and would do what is necessary to protect its rights. The ministry also added that sanctions and pressure tactics do not help resolve problems. How has Iran responded to the new sanctions? Over the weekend, the head of Iran's top security body warned that Tehran would see any country's support of the US measures as an "act of war." Supreme National Security Council leader Mohsen Rezaei said Iran would "retaliate in a seismic manner" to the sanctions by targeting other oil-shipping routes from the Persian Gulf. "If the economic war ​continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported , neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf," Rezaei said. The current situation in the Iran war The Middle East war began on February 28 when Israel and the US carried out strikes on Iran, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei . Tehran responded with strikes on energy infrastructure and US bases in the Gulf region. While the two sides have stopped the bombing, talks to end the conflict have stalled, with control over the Strait of Hormuz remaining a key sticking point. Iran has effectively closed the waterway , crucial for global oil and gas shipments, while the US maintains a blockade of Iranian ports. Under a memorandum of understanding signed in June, the two sides had 60 days to negotiate an end to the war and reach an agreement on Iran's nuclear program. But that period expired last week with no signs of a deal. Meanwhile, Pakistan's army chief was expected to travel to Iran on Monday as part of efforts to revive diplomatic talks in the conflict. And on Tuesday, Oman's foreign minister is set meet his Iranian counterpart to continue talks on the Strait of Hormuz. Can Pakistan still help end the US-Iran war? https://www.politico.eu/article/hungary-.text: Hungary has ordered the expulsion of 10 Russian diplomats to protect its “security and sovereignty,” the country’s Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Orbán announced Tuesday. The decision comes several months after Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo reported that nearly one-third of the Russian embassy’s 47 staff members in Budapest have links to Russian intelligence . Orbán — no relation to former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán — said the diplomats “had engaged in activities in Hungary that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention,” the international treaty setting the principles of diplomatic relations. Advertisement Advertisement Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar also said the diplomats “have committed unacceptable activities in Hungary.” Neither he nor Orbán specified the nature of their allegations. The Hungarian foreign ministry declined to make further comments. The move “does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia,” Orbán said. Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said Moscow’s response would be “harsh and painful,” according to Russian state news agency Interfax . Magyar has sought to sever ties with Moscow since taking over from Viktor Orbán in May, a sharp shift from his predecessor’s coziness with the Kremlin . In July, authorities opened an investigation into former Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó over allegations that he shared sensitive information with Russian officials. In August, Magyar’s government said Russia was “a threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order” to Hungary, Europe and the global order” in its instructions to Hungary’s delegation to the U.N. Courtesy the artist and Capsule Shanghai. LONG ISLAND CITY, NY .- SculptureCenter announced the artists selected through our In Practice 2027 Open Call for Artist Proposals: Jianxin Tian, Thomas Tait, Anastasia Sosunova, Ash Moniz, Max Popov, and Jessica Wilson. In Practice: Jianxin Tian On View: Jan 27–Mar 8, 2027 Often combining mythological or whimsical motifs with elements of industrial design, Jianxin Tian hammers reliefs onto mass-produced metal objects, as if enchanting the mundane world. Tian presses and chisels sensual bodily forms onto domestic objects, continuing an initial motivation to draw out a poetics of kitchenware that formed during the pandemic lockdown. His practice, grounded in his training in Greco-Roman classical and modernist sculpture, is propelled by an urge to contend with the iconography of everyday life. For In Practice, Tian expands from household items to working with parts from large-scale industrial production, creating forms that diverge from the aesthetics of the assembly line. In Practice: Thomas Tait On View: Mar–Apr 2027 Immersed in the language of puppetry, Thomas Tait’s work borrows world-building methods from set design and kinetics thinking from performance. Often held in the fragile equilibrium of a complex system, Tait’s figurines are composed of found and organic materials. The visibility of the inner supporting structure and the unpredictability of their movement suggest an interiority to the figurines, inviting ontological speculation. For In Practice, Tait will develop a marionette pulley system organized around a central armature. By amplifying the friction within the installation, Tait’s DIY engineering explores whether a conscious "ghost" can arise from a structural apparatus. In Practice: Anastasia Sosunova On View: May–Jun 2027 Working between video, printmaking, and sculpture, Anastasia Sosunova shapes installations that draw upon shared rituals and mythologies that mobilize community thinking. Her projects address themes related to the coexistence of seemingly incompatible value systems. Over the last few years, she has centered in on the Lithuanian chain Senukai (a DIY retail empire), which leans into the vulnerabilities produced by a precarious national economy, marketing the ideal of self-sufficiency. Negotiating the romantic yet futile promises of hardware stores, Sosunova will build an environment that evokes both the anarchic logic of the hand-built and a moody Eastern European futurism for In Practice. The work emerges from the artist’s research into the contemporary shortage of homebuilding supplies, which has been intensified by the expansion of the defense industries across NATO countries. In Practice: Ash Moniz On View: Jul–Aug 2027 Ash Moniz is an artist whose work centers on the refusal to appear within artistic and political contexts that often desire personal representation, regardless of its costs. Her In Practice exhibition gives new form to a number of long-term artistic relationships and open-ended international projects made with subjects who cannot (or, for their own safety, choose not to) identify themselves due to their positions within conditions of war, precarious labor, and activism. The resulting works—in sculpture, installation, video, and text—document a compounding absence of representability within Moniz’s broader practice. Her attempt to describe and connect such voids through artworks reflects a tense negotiation of trust, agency, safety, and solidarity that underpins both artistic and political expression in this time. In Practice: Max Popov On View: Sep–Oct 2027 Max Popov reconstitutes obsolete and cast-aside materials, creating sculptures and installations that carry layered messages of both remembrance and the potential for renewal. Both elegiac and speculative, his work reveals how time accumulates as residue, and exposes the mutability of progress and permanence. For In Practice, Popov will create a new installation composed from the remnants of daily life—the material aftermath of objects after their value has been extracted or exhausted—and the impressions they leave behind. In Practice: Jessica Wilson On View: Nov–Dec 2027 Through animation, sculpture, and installation, Jessica Wilson explores the somatic and material effects of virtual systems—rendering unseen forces palpable through light, color, and spatial parameters. Her practice contends with the competing desires to index technical processes and to charge them with emotion, a tension that finds expression in physical sensation. For In Practice, she turns to disused LED taxi tops salvaged from New York City cabs, reviving the onboard advertisements from when she found them as ghostly echoes, while adding new animations that might expose the machine’s inner turmoil—a cartoonish live-feed MRI of processing and transmitting. The work embeds the taxi tops, normally used for targeted ads, with an imagined inner life, turning their components into protagonists of their own dramatic days.
